subject: mathematics
question_text: By the Gauss-Jordan method, solve 3x + 4y + 5z = 18, 2x − y + 8z = 13, 5x − 2y + 7z = 20.

mark_split.label: Clear column 1 below the leading entry
Reach a leading 1 in the last row

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.33 — LAQ chapter 3 Matrices, answer 20.2, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). Printed appearances: TS 15. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S. Book p.33 sets two Gauss-Jordan questions side by side in two columns, leaving no margin for the [N Marks] tags the chapter uses elsewhere, so no split is printed for any Gauss-Jordan answer. The 1+2+1+2+1 above follows the only split this book states for a solving-a-system question — the note on book p.30 reading 'Just finding A⁻¹ gives u 4 Marks. For remaining steps u get 3 Marks' — by weighting the bulk row-reduction (4 marks across clearing down and clearing up) against the setup and the finish (3 marks). ⚠ THE ROW-OPERATION CHAIN IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S. Book p.33 prints this answer in a narrow second column and two of its operation annotations could not be read off the scan with confidence (the printed page gives a row of −680 where the working above reaches −136). Rather than transcribe an uncertain sequence, a clean chain was authored here and each of its eleven operations checked by hand; the final solution x=3, y=1, z=1 agrees with the book's, and with this unit's Cramer and matrix-inversion answers for the SAME system. Any valid row-reduction reaches the same answer, so this is a presentation choice, not a correction. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on both unique-solution Gauss-Jordan answers in this unit. The two remaining Gauss-Jordan answers, 20.3 and 20.4, do NOT share this skeleton: their systems have an infinite solution set and no solution respectively, so their closing steps are a different argument. Star rank is the CHAPTER's ★★★, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to the "Clear upwards to the identity" step.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by the Gauss-Jordan method — say what matrix you write down first, which direction you clear in, and how you get the answer at the end.

steps.label: Write the augmented matrix
steps.margin_note: First mark. The augmented matrix is A with the constants column joined on. The rule down the middle is not decoration — it marks where the equals sign was, and every row operation acts across it.
steps.memory_tip: A with the constants attached; the rule down the middle marks the equals sign.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 4 & 5 \\ 2 & -1 & 8 \\ 5 & -2 & 7 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 18 \\ 13 \\ 20 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the augmented matrix [A | D] is written — the coefficient matrix with the constants column attached.
accept: write the augmented matrix A D with the constants joined on to the coefficient matrix
form A given D by putting the right hand side as a fourth column
write the coefficient matrix together with the constants column
augmented matrix rasta, coefficients tho patu constants column kuda
attach the constants to A to make the augmented matrix

steps.why: Every row of the augmented matrix IS one of the original equations. That is why a row operation is legal — adding one equation to another never changes the solution set.
common_mistakes: Writing A alone and doing the row operations without the constants.
Putting the constants in as a fourth ROW instead of a fourth column.
Writing the coefficients in the order they appear rather than in x, y, z order.

steps.label: Clear column 1
steps.margin_note: Two marks. No entry in column 1 is a 1, but R₁ − R₂ makes one — 3 − 2 = 1. Hunting for a leading 1 before clearing the column is what keeps this question free of fractions.
steps.memory_tip: No entry in column 1 is a 1, but R₁ − R₂ makes one — 3 − 2 = 1. Hunt for a leading 1 first.
lines: R₁ → R₁ − R₂  (to get a leading 1)

recall.must_convey: That a leading 1 is obtained in the top-left position and then used to make the rest of column 1 zero.
accept: get a one in the top left corner then subtract multiples of row one to make the rest of the first column zero
use the leading one to clear column one below it
make the first column zeros under the leading entry using row operations
first column lo leading one techi, kinda unna entries ni zero chestham
swap or subtract to get a one on top then knock out the entries below it

steps.why: Gauss-Jordan works one column at a time, and it always wants a 1 at the pivot first. Chasing zeros before you have that 1 is what forces fractions into the working.
common_mistakes: Starting to clear the column before securing a leading 1 and drowning in fractions.
Applying an operation to only part of a row — every entry moves, including the constant.
Changing the pivot row while using it to clear the others.

steps.label: Reach a leading 1 in R₃
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Once row 3 reads 0 0 1 with a number after the rule, z is already known — everything from here is bookkeeping to get x and y out.
steps.memory_tip: Once row 3 reads 0 0 1 with a number after the rule, z is already known.

recall.must_convey: That the last row is reduced to 0, 0, 1 with the value of z after the rule — that is, the third pivot is made 1.
accept: reduce the last row to zero zero one so that z is read directly
make the third pivot a one by dividing the row
get the bottom row to zero zero one which gives z
last row ni zero zero one ga marchali, appudu z telustundi
divide the bottom row so the pivot becomes one and z is known

steps.why: This is the point where Gauss elimination would stop and back-substitute. Gauss-Jordan carries on and clears upwards too, which is why the answer needs no substitution at all.
common_mistakes: Dividing the row by the wrong entry.
Dividing the coefficients but not the constant after the rule.
Stopping here and calling it the answer; only z is known so far.

steps.label: Clear upwards
steps.margin_note: Three marks. Every pivot is a 1 by this point, so clearing upwards is pure addition. Work from the bottom row up: use row 3 to clear column 3, then row 2 to clear column 2.
steps.memory_tip: Every pivot is a 1 by now, so clearing upwards is pure addition. Work from the bottom row up.

recall.must_convey: That the elimination is then run upwards — using the lower rows to clear the entries ABOVE the pivots, until only the diagonal is left.
accept: now clear upwards using the bottom row to remove the entries above the pivots
work from the bottom up making the entries above each pivot zero
eliminate above the diagonal so only the pivots are left
ippudu paina unna entries ni kuda zero chestham, kinda nunchi paiki
use row three then row two to clear everything above them

steps.why: Clearing upwards as well as downwards is the ONLY difference between Gauss-Jordan and plain Gauss elimination. It buys you an answer you can read straight off, with no back-substitution.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the triangular form and back-substituting; that is Gauss, not Gauss-Jordan.
Clearing upwards before the pivots are 1, which reintroduces fractions.
Forgetting to carry the operation across the rule into the constant.

steps.label: Read off the solution
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Each row is now a one-letter equation, so the answer is read straight off with no substitution.
steps.memory_tip: Each row is a one-letter equation — read the answer straight off.
lines: Each row is now a single equation:

recall.must_convey: That each row of the reduced matrix reads as one equation, giving x = 3, y = 1, z = 1.
accept: each row is now one equation so read x y and z straight off
the reduced matrix gives the values directly with no substitution
read the answers from the last column
prathi row oke equation kabatti x y z direct ga chadavachu
the three rows give the three unknowns immediately

steps.why: A row reading 0 0 1 | 3 is literally the equation z = 3. Understanding that the matrix never stopped being the equations is what makes the whole method feel less like a trick.
common_mistakes: Reading the values in the wrong order.
Forgetting a row left with a −1 pivot, which needs one sign flip.
Never substituting back to check — x=3, y=1, z=1 in the first equation gives 9+4+5 = 18.

insider_note: R₁ − R₂ produces a leading 1 with no fractions, which is worth doing before anything else. The numbers grow large in the middle but come back to 3, 1 and 1.
